newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM struggles to retain power as pressure mounts.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM struggles to retain power as pressure mounts.

text.p: Embattled Thai Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa is struggling to maintain his leadership as political pressure from within his coalition and opposition mounts ahead of a no-confidence debate against him next week.

Political analysts said on Monday Banharn, rated as having the lowest popularity for a Thai leader in two decades, also faced problems from poor Thai economic indicators that put the baht and stock market under heavy pressure in the past week.
"I would bet on Banharn ending up resigning. He's becoming more isolated by the day and has lost all bargaining power," said lecturer Chira Hongladarom of Thammasat University.
"He is being squeezed from all sides, politically and economically," he said.

Banharn is accused by the opposition of economic mismanagement and plagiarism involving a thesis for his master's law degree. He has denied the accusations and vowed to fight them at the September 18 debate on the no-confidence motion.
Thai stocks, hit by sluggish exports and the slowest Thai economic growth in a decade, have lost 11 percent since August 29 and wallowed at near three-year lows.
The baht has since late July weathered sporadic attacks in local and foreign money markets as dealers speculate that Thailand may resort to devaluing the currency to help exports.

"The opposition has an easy task (in the no-confidence debate). It has a wide array of issues to pick from. Even our strong economy is facing depression that we have not witnessed before," said Somjai Phagaphasvivat of Thammasat University.
Banharn has faced calls for his resignation in recent weeks from the opposition, some politicians in his coalition, and from some in a normally neutral business community.
"Banharn's resignation could help lift market sentiment," said Somsak Boonsupaporn, United Securities Corp's vice president for research, reflecting the opinion of brokers.

Two parties in Banharn's six-party coalition, which enjoys a slim 13-vote majority in the 391-seat lower House of Representatives, have said their support for him would hinge on how he fares during the no-confidence debate.

Analysts said the two partners -- the 57-seat New Aspiration Party led by Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh and the 18-seat Nam Thai Party led by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Amnuay Viravan -- hold the key to Banharn's survival.
"Chavalit holds the trump card. He is the kingmaker who can make or break Banharn. I have a feeling Banharn will get a hard landing on his way out," Chira of Thammasat said.
"Chavalit would probably meet Banharn on the eve of the no-confidence vote (expected after the debate on September 20) to name his price for backing him," an analyst said.

Analysts said however that Chavalit, a former army chief, may choose to delay fulfilling his long-standing ambition to be prime minister in return for politicial concessions he can extract from Banharn.
Chavalit has in the past week floated a proposal for Banharn to appoint a high-power "economic dream team," headed by his close ally Amnuay, to reverse the Thai economic slump.
Banharn has long reserved key finance, commerce and interior portfolios for his own Chart Thai Party.
Although Amnuay has been Banharn's deputy in charge of macro-economic policies and foreign trade, he has not been given real power to set budgets or supervise the central bank.

Analysts said Chavalit may back Amnuay, a respected banker and former finance minister, as a temporary prime minister should Banharn step down while the former army general takes time brushing up his public image.

"Amnuay would make a good stand-in for prime minister, say for six months. He should be acceptable to Moody's," said Chira, referring to the credit rating agency's decision last week to downgrade Thailand's short-term debt ratings.
